Our view is not that surprisal (or any other metric extracted from an LLM) is inherently informative about which representations or mechanisms underlie human language comprehension—or, for that matter, LLMs themselves. Similarly, measures of human behavior (e.g., reading time) or brain activity (e.g., EEG amplitude) are not inherently meaningful. Indeed, in virtually all areas of scientific investigation, a measured variable is interpretable only in the light of appropriate theoretical scaffolding and study design, even if that theoretical scaffolding is relatively minimal, e.g., an assumption that processing difficulty is correlated with reading time. Concretely: first, there must be a plausible link between some theoretical construct and the measured variable in question; and second, this variable must be analyzed in terms of some other theoretically meaningful variable, e.g., an experimental manipulation intended to shed light on a research question.

paras.sec_title: Objection: Neural Language Models are Difficult to Interpret
paras.text: Although language models are built and trained by humans, the internal mechanisms that give rise to their behavior are not easily interpretable from their architecture or parameters alone. This is why such models are occasionally called “opaque” or “black boxes”. Indeed, the field of “mechanistic interpretability” (Olah et al., 2020; Sharkey et al., 2025) exists primarily because of this opacity, and is dedicated to identifying the circuits and representations underlying behavior. This field has made some progress, e.g., in cataloging the putative functions of different attention heads (Edelman et al., 2024; Htut et al., 2019; Olsson et al., 2022), but a complete accounting (in either psychological or mechanistic terms) of LLM behavior remains elusive. Thus, one concern might be that even if distributional predictability succeeds in partially or fully explaining away an experimental manipulation, we will not be able to determine why. This is further complicated by the observation that distributional predictability likely reflects other relevant psycholinguistic variables, such as frequency, concreteness, or even age of acquisition, meaning that a “successful” baseline result cannot necessarily be attributed to distributional predictability per se. (See also “Surprisal is a metric, not a mechanism”, as well as “Are LLMs too good?”.)

paras.sec_title: Objection: Neural Language Models are Difficult to Interpret
paras.text: Finally, the fact that distributional predictability may covary with other variables of interest (such as unigram frequency) is also not a fundamental problem for the baselines approach. As noted above, the goal of the baselines approach is to answer the following question: does an experimental manipulation account for variance in human behavior above and beyond that explained by distributional predictability? Answering this question is not undermined by the fact that surprisal correlates with other variables, provided the researcher is careful not to make specific mechanistic claims about surprisal as the particular causal mechanism driving human behavior. Our case is more modest: a “successful” baselines result does not provide evidence that surprisal causes an effect, but rather serves as an index of what is achievable through exposure to distributional statistics. Just as unigram frequency might constitute an alternative causal explanation for an effect, distributional predictability represents another such alternative. Moreover, the fact that surprisal correlates with other variables could be taken as a sign of its utility and predictive power. Of course, we do encourage researchers who wish to disentangle the effect of surprisal from other variables (such as frequency) to do so, e.g., as in Goodkind and Bicknell (2021).

We also anticipate several more general applications of language models as distributional baselines. First, language models offer a degree of control and access that is impossible with human participants. In principle, researchers can control which data a model is trained on, allowing researchers to test questions about what kinds of input is required to form which kinds of generalizations (Misra & Mahowald, 2024; Yao et al., 2025); in some cases, this approach could even be used to generate novel hypotheses, which could in turn be tested in human participants (Misra & Kim, 2024). Similarly, the internal states of language models can be directly probed and even manipulated, allowing researchers to test questions about the representations and mechanisms that give rise to model behaviors (Marks et al., 2024; Olsson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022). While work on language model interpretability is still arguably “pre-paradigmatic” (Olah et al., 2020), it represents another promising direction for testing hypotheses that cannot be directly assessed in humans. In this way, language models could be used as a kind of “model organism” to establish convergent evidence for certain research questions in psycholinguistics.

This notion of language models as “model organisms” connects to another possible future direction, which expands beyond the use of text-only models to models trained on a variety of modalities. Naturally, a model trained on both text data and images (i.e., a “vision-language model” or VLM) should not be used as an operationalization of theories about linguistic input specifically. Yet these models could be used as implementations of distinct theories about whether and to what extent linguistic representations are grounded with non-linguistic information (Barsalou, 1999; Bergen, 2015; Glenberg & Kaschak, 2002). Indeed, recent work has already begun comparing the psychometric predictive power of text-only language models to models exposed to visual information, though in practice visual grounding does not always improve psychometric predictive power (Bavaresco et al., 2024; Bavaresco & Fernández, 2025; Jones et al., 2024c; Jones & Trott, 2024). In theory, modifying the training regime and architecture of these VLMs could allow researchers to test questions about multimodal conceptual integration in humans.

Note that tokens are generally assigned using compression algorithms such as byte-pair encoding (Sennrich et al., 2016) that allows the vocabulary of the model to effectively cover all possible text sequences, with more common sequences of bytes generally being merged into tokens. Thus, some (generally more common) words are represented by one token, while others are represented by sequences of sub-word tokens.
